headline: Microsoft Outage Forces Millions to Communicate Using Ancient 'Speech' Technology
subheadline: With Teams and Outlook down worldwide, office workers report being obliged to 'walk over' and 'say words' to colleagues, a practice experts believe dates back millennia.
author: Basil Farthingale, Senior Technology Correspondent
seoTitle: Microsoft 365 Outage Forces Workers to Speak Out Loud | The Daily Absurd
seoDescription: Satire: a global Microsoft 365 outage left millions without Teams or Outlook, forcing the rediscovery of face-to-face conversation. Experts are horrified.
sourceEvent: A global Microsoft 365 outage on 12–13 November 2026 disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for roughly 24 hours; Microsoft blamed a network capacity upgrade and stressed it was not caused by AI.

altHeadlines: IT Departments Worldwide Enjoy Quietest Day on Record
Outage Leaves Workers With No Option But to Do Actual Work

body:
Offices on every continent descended into chaos and, bafflingly, productivity this week after a global Microsoft 365 outage severed humanity's access to Outlook, Teams and Copilot for nearly 24 hours.

With digital communication severed, workers worldwide were forced to fall back on what anthropologists describe as 'the before methods': walking to a colleague's desk, speaking words into the air, and in extreme cases, telephoning.

"I walked twenty metres to ask Priya a question," said one shaken London accounts manager. "She answered immediately. There was no 'typing…' indicator. No way to leave her on read. I don't know how our ancestors coped."

Airlines, courts, schools and governments all reported disruption, with several emergency meetings convened to discuss the outage, which attendees described as 'weirdly efficient' due to the absence of anyone saying "you're on mute".

Microsoft assured the public the failure was caused by a routine network capacity upgrade and was 'definitely not related to AI or agents', a clarification that calmed absolutely no one, since it implies the machines were innocent this time and the humans simply tripped over a cable.

Early reports suggest the outage had unexpected side effects. Three multinational corporations accidentally held stand-up meetings that stood up. A Geneva diplomacy summit concluded forty minutes early. Somewhere in Ohio, a man is said to have finished a task.

"The most disturbing thing we saw," said a crisis response coordinator, "was employees looking out of windows. Some reported seeing a 'sky'. Others described a large burning light. We are treating these accounts as unverified."

At press time, service had been restored and humanity had unanimously agreed to never speak of the incident again, except in twelve separate Teams channels dedicated to speaking about it.
